PAY SCALE DISCLOSURE AND SALARY HISTORY BAN — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

ABOUT THIS PAY SCALE DISCLOSURE AND SALARY HISTORY BAN INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes two related California Labor Code requirements that can arise in Acme Manufacturing, Inc.'s hiring process for Morgan T. Ellis in connection with the position of Warehouse Associate: the statutory ban on relying on, or asking about, an applicant's salary history, and the statutory duty to disclose a position's pay scale under specified circumstances, including in job postings. It summarizes selected requirements of California Labor Code section 432.3, and, where relevant, section 1197.5. It is not a determination that any specific question asked, information sought, pay scale disclosed or withheld, or job posting drafted by Acme Manufacturing, Inc. in connection with Morgan T. Ellis or the Warehouse Associate position complies or fails to comply with either statute, and it does not itself satisfy any notice, posting, or recordkeeping duty either statute may impose.

THE SALARY HISTORY BAN: TWO SEPARATE PROHIBITIONS, APPLICABLE TO ALL EMPLOYERS
California law imposes two separate prohibitions on an employer in connection with an applicant's salary history: an employer may not rely on an applicant's salary history information as a factor in deciding whether to offer employment or what salary to offer, and, separately, an employer may not seek salary history information about an applicant, whether orally or in writing, and whether personally or through an agent. The statute states that it applies to all employers, including state and local government employers and the Legislature, without any numerical size threshold.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall not rely on the salary history information of an applicant for employment as a factor in determining whether to offer employment to an applicant or what salary to offer an applicant."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, ban on relying on salary history in hiring/salary decisions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "An employer shall not, orally or in writing, personally or through an agent, seek salary history information, including compensation and benefits, about an applicant for employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, ban on seeking salary history information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "This section applies to all employers, including state and local government employers and the Legislature."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(g) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, section applies to all employers regardless of size (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(a), (b), and (g)), used as real evidence of California's salary-history-ban requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's actual situation. All three citations below are to subdivisions (a), (b), and (g) of a single statutory section, Section 432.3; they are treated here as one source describing the ban and its scope, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific question asked or not asked, or any specific hiring decision made, by any particular employer complied or failed to comply with Section 432.3(a) or (b), and does not determine that any particular employer's practices toward any particular applicant or employee are compliant or noncompliant with it.

EXCEPTIONS: VOLUNTARY DISCLOSURE, SALARY-EXPECTATION QUESTIONS, AND THE LINK TO THE EQUAL PAY ACT
The salary-history ban does not prohibit an applicant from voluntarily and without prompting disclosing salary history information to a prospective employer, and if an applicant does so, the statute does not prohibit that employer from considering or relying on that voluntarily disclosed information in determining the applicant's salary. Separately, the statute does not prohibit an employer from asking an applicant about the applicant's salary expectation for the position being applied for. The statute also cross-references California's Equal Pay Act, stating that, consistent with Labor Code section 1197.5, nothing in the salary-history-ban statute is to be construed to allow prior salary to justify any disparity in compensation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Nothing in this section shall prohibit an applicant from voluntarily and without prompting disclosing salary history information to a prospective employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, voluntary-and-unprompted-disclosure exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "If an applicant voluntarily and without prompting discloses salary history information to a prospective employer, nothing in this section shall prohibit that employer from considering or relying on that voluntarily disclosed salary history information in determining the salary for that applicant."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employer may consider voluntarily disclosed salary history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "Nothing in this section shall prohibit an employer from asking an applicant about the applicant’s salary expectation for the position being applied for."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employer may ask about salary expectations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "Consistent with Section 1197.5, nothing in this section shall be construed to allow prior salary to justify any disparity in compensation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(k) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, cross-reference to Section 1197.5 on prior salary and pay disparity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(h), (i), (j), and (k)), used as real evidence of these exceptions and cross-reference — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All four citations below are to subdivisions (h) through (k) of a single statutory section, Section 432.3; they are treated here as one source describing related exceptions and a cross-reference, not as independent corroborating sources. The fourth citation, subdivision (k), points to Labor Code section 1197.5 rather than restating its text; a separate clause in this information sheet addresses what Section 1197.5 itself says and, as importantly, what it does not say about job postings. This clause does not determine whether any particular disclosure by any particular applicant to any particular employer was, in fact, voluntary and without prompting, and is informational only: it does not determine that any particular employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 432.3.

DUTY TO DISCLOSE PAY SCALE ON REQUEST — APPLICANTS AND CURRENT EMPLOYEES, NO SIZE THRESHOLD
Separately from any job posting, California law requires an employer, upon reasonable request, to provide the pay scale for a position to an applicant applying for that position, and requires an employer, upon request, to provide a current employee the pay scale for the position in which that employee is currently employed. By their own text, neither of these two request-triggered disclosure duties is limited to employers of any particular size.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer, upon reasonable request, shall provide the pay scale for a position to an applicant applying for employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, pay scale to applicant upon reasonable request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "An employer, upon request, shall provide an employee the pay scale for the position in which the employee is currently employed."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, pay scale to current employee upon request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(c)(1) and (c)(2)), used as real evidence of these request-triggered pay-scale disclosure duties — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to paragraphs (1) and (2) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 432.3(c); they are treated here as one source describing two related disclosure duties, not as independent corroborating sources. A separate clause in this information sheet addresses the different, proactive job-posting disclosure duty in Section 432.3(c)(3) and (c)(5), which does carry a 15-employee threshold; this clause does not state that the two duties are identical in scope. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific request made or not made, or any specific pay-scale figure disclosed or withheld, by any particular employer toward any particular applicant or employee satisfied or failed to satisfy Section 432.3(c)(1) or (c)(2).

JOB-POSTING PAY SCALE REQUIREMENT AND THE 15-EMPLOYEE THRESHOLD
California law requires an employer with 15 or more employees to include the pay scale for a position in any job posting for that position. If such an employer engages a third party to announce, post, publish, or otherwise make known a job posting, the employer must provide the pay scale to that third party, and the third party must include the pay scale in the job posting.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer with 15 or more employees shall include the pay scale for a position in any job posting."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, pay scale in job postings for employers with 15+ employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "An employer with 15 or more employees that engages a third party to announce, post, publish, or otherwise make known a job posting shall provide the pay scale to the third party. The third party shall include the pay scale in the job posting."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, third-party job-posting pay scale duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(c)(3) and (c)(5)), used as real evidence of the job-posting pay-scale requirement and its numerical threshold — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to paragraphs (3) and (5) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 432.3(c); they are treated here as one source describing a proactive posting duty and its extension to third-party postings, not as independent corroborating sources. This 15-employee threshold applies specifically to these two paragraphs; a separate clause in this information sheet addresses the request-triggered disclosure duties in Section 432.3(c)(1) and (c)(2), which by their own text carry no such threshold, and this clause does not state or imply that every duty this statute creates shares the same size threshold. The statute does not itself define how an employer's number of employees is counted (for example, whether part-time employees, employees outside California, or a particular measurement date are included), and this clause does not resolve that question or determine that any particular employer does or does not meet the threshold. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific job posting used by any particular employer for any particular position complied or failed to comply with Section 432.3(c)(3) or (c)(5).

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: “PAY SCALE” AND “APPLICANT”
The statute defines "pay scale" to mean a good faith estimate of the salary or hourly wage range that the employer reasonably expects to pay for the position upon hire. It defines "applicant" or "applicant for employment" to mean an individual who is seeking employment with the employer and who is not currently employed with that employer in any capacity or position.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Pay scale” means a good faith estimate of the salary or hourly wage range that the employer reasonably expects to pay for the position upon hire."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(m)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of “pay scale” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "“Applicant” or “applicant for employment” means an individual who is seeking employment with the employer and is not currently employed with that employer in any capacity or position."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(m)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of “applicant” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(m)(1) and (m)(2)), used as real evidence of these two statutory definitions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to paragraphs (1) and (2) of a single statutory subdivision, Section 432.3(m); they are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. The pay-scale definition turns on the employer's own good faith estimate of a range it reasonably expects to pay, rather than on any fixed formula, and this clause does not determine what dollar figures any particular employer does or should reasonably expect to pay for any particular position. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular figure or range disclosed by any particular employer does or does not meet this statutory definition of "pay scale."

RECORDKEEPING DUTY, CIVIL PENALTIES, AND ENFORCEMENT PROCEDURE
The statute requires an employer to maintain records of a job title and wage rate history for each employee for the duration of that employment plus three years after the employment ends, so that the Labor Commissioner can determine whether a pattern of wage discrepancy still exists; these records must be open to inspection by the Labor Commissioner. A person claiming to be aggrieved by a violation of the statute may file a written complaint with the Labor Commissioner within one year after learning of the violation, stating the employer's name and address and a detailed account of the alleged violation, and may separately bring a civil action for injunctive relief and any other relief the court deems appropriate. The Labor Commissioner must promptly investigate complaints alleging a violation, and upon finding a violation, may order the employer to pay a civil penalty of not less than $100 and not more than $10,000 per violation, with the amount based on the totality of the circumstances, including whether the employer has previously violated the section; for a first violation of the job-posting subdivision specifically, no penalty is assessed if the employer demonstrates that all job postings for open positions have been updated to include the required pay scale. If an employer fails to keep the required records, the statute creates a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee's claim.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall maintain records of a job title and wage rate history for each employee for the duration of the employment plus three years after the end of the employment in order for the Labor Commissioner to determine if there is still a pattern of wage discrepancy. These records shall be open to inspection by the Labor Commissioner."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(c)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, job title and wage rate history recordkeeping duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "A person who claims to be aggrieved by a violation of this section may file a written complaint with the Labor Commissioner within one year after the date the person learned of the violation. The complaint shall state the name and address of the employer and shall provide a detailed account of the alleged violation, as may be required by the Labor Commissioner."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, written complaint to the Labor Commissioner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "A person who claims to be aggrieved by a violation of this section may also bring a civil action for injunctive relief and any other relief that the court deems appropriate."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, private civil action for injunctive relief (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "The Labor Commissioner shall promptly investigate complaints alleging violation of this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner's duty to investigate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "Upon finding that an employer has violated this section, the Labor Commissioner may order the employer to pay a civil penalty of no less than one hundred dollars ($100) and no more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per violation. The Labor Commissioner shall determine the amount of the penalty based on the totality of the circumstances, including, but not limited to, whether the employer has previously violated this section. For a first violation of subdivision (c), no penalty shall be assessed upon demonstration by the employer that all job postings for open positions have been updated to include the pay scale as required by this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(d)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, civil penalty range and first-violation cure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  "If an employer fails to keep records in violation of this section, there shall be a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee’s claim."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 432.3(d)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, rebuttable presumption for failure to keep records (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.3.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432.3(c)(4) and (d)(1) through (d)(5)), used as real evidence of California's recordkeeping duty, complaint and civil-action procedures, civil penalty range, and adverse-inference-style presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. All six citations below are to a single paragraph, (c)(4), and paragraphs (1) through (5) of a single statutory subdivision, (d), of one section, Section 432.3; they are treated here as one source describing one connected recordkeeping-and-enforcement scheme, not as independent corroborating sources. By its own text, the recordkeeping duty in paragraph (c)(4) carries no 15-employee threshold and so is not, on its face, limited to the same employers as the job-posting duty in (c)(3); this clause does not resolve any tension that might arise from that reading. The first-violation cure applies, by its own text, only to a violation "of subdivision (c)" — the pay-scale provisions — and this clause does not state that the same cure applies to a violation of the separate salary-history-ban provisions in subdivisions (a) or (b). This clause does not identify any reported court decision applying the civil penalty or the recordkeeping presumption, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer has or has not kept the required records for any particular employee, and does not determine that any employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 432.3.

LABOR CODE § 1197.5: CALIFORNIA'S EQUAL PAY ACT, NOT THE SOURCE OF THE JOB-POSTING DUTY
Labor Code section 1197.5 is California's Equal Pay Act. Its own text prohibits paying an employee at a wage rate less than the rate paid to an employee of another sex (and, separately, another race or ethnicity) for substantially similar work, unless the employer demonstrates that the entire wage differential is accounted for by specified factors, and it states that prior salary alone shall not justify a pay disparity. It also requires every employer to maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of its employees, on file for three years. Section 1197.5's own text does not contain a requirement that an employer include a pay scale in a job posting; the job-posting pay-scale requirement, its 15-employee threshold, and the related third-party-posting duty appear in Labor Code section 432.3, not in section 1197.5.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Prior salary shall not justify any disparity in compensation. Nothing in this section shall be interpreted to mean that an employer may not make a compensation decision based on a current employee’s existing salary, so long as any wage differential resulting from that compensation decision is justified by one or more of the factors in this subdivision."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Equal Pay Act sex-based wage-differential prohibition and prior-salary limitation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "Every employer shall maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of the persons employed by the employer. All of the records shall be kept on file for a period of three years."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Equal Pay Act general wage/job-classification recordkeeping duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(a) and (e)), used as real evidence of what Section 1197.5 itself requires and does not require — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to subdivisions (a) and (e) of a single statutory section, Section 1197.5; they are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause's drafter read Section 1197.5 in full, subdivisions (a) through (l), and confirmed that no part of its current codified text imposes a job-posting pay-scale disclosure duty of the kind found in Section 432.3(c)(3) and (c)(5); this is an absence found by reading the entire section, not an absence inferred from a partial reading. This clause does not restate every element of the Equal Pay Act's burden-shifting framework in subdivision (a), and does not determine whether any specific pay differential between any particular employees is or is not justified under Section 1197.5. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's pay practices toward any particular employee are compliant or noncompliant with Section 1197.5.

expectedJSON.body: The statute requires an employer to maintain records of a job title and wage rate history for each employee for the duration of that employment plus three years after the employment ends, so that the Labor Commissioner can determine whether a pattern of wage discrepancy still exists; these records must be open to inspection by the Labor Commissioner. A person claiming to be aggrieved by a violation of the statute may file a written complaint with the Labor Commissioner within one year after learning of the violation, stating the employer's name and address and a detailed account of the alleged violation, and may separately bring a civil action for injunctive relief and any other relief the court deems appropriate. The Labor Commissioner must promptly investigate complaints alleging a violation, and upon finding a violation, may order the employer to pay a civil penalty of not less than $100 and not more than $10,000 per violation, with the amount based on the totality of the circumstances, including whether the employer has previously violated the section; for a first violation of the job-posting subdivision specifically, no penalty is assessed if the employer demonstrates that all job postings for open positions have been updated to include the required pay scale. If an employer fails to keep the required records, the statute creates a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee's claim.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code section 1197.5 is California's Equal Pay Act. Its own text prohibits paying an employee at a wage rate less than the rate paid to an employee of another sex (and, separately, another race or ethnicity) for substantially similar work, unless the employer demonstrates that the entire wage differential is accounted for by specified factors, and it states that prior salary alone shall not justify a pay disparity. It also requires every employer to maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of its employees, on file for three years. Section 1197.5's own text does not contain a requirement that an employer include a pay scale in a job posting; the job-posting pay-scale requirement, its 15-employee threshold, and the related third-party-posting duty appear in Labor Code section 432.3, not in section 1197.5.
